q: What is Ansible and how does its agentless architecture work?
a: Ansible is an automation tool for configuration management, application deployment and orchestration. A control node reads an inventory of target hosts and a playbook, which is a YAML description of desired state. For each task it generates a small module, copies it to the target over SSH or WinRM, runs it with the target's Python interpreter, collects the JSON result and removes the temporary files. Because nothing permanent is installed, there is no agent to patch, no extra port to open and no central server required, which makes onboarding fast and the attack surface small. The trade-offs are that SSH round trips cost time at large scale, the control node needs network reach to every host, and Python is needed on managed Linux hosts. Modules are designed to be idempotent, so running the same playbook twice should change nothing the second time.
f: What does a module run look like on the target?
When would you choose an agent-based tool instead?
p: A control node pushes small modules over SSH or WinRM, runs them, returns JSON and cleans up. No agent is installed, which keeps onboarding easy and the attack surface small, at the cost of SSH latency at very large scale.
tip: Say agentless plus idempotent modules, and name the scale trade-off.

q: What is an inventory, and how do static and dynamic inventories differ?
a: An inventory tells Ansible which hosts exist and how they are grouped. A static inventory is an INI or YAML file listing hosts and groups, with variables attached to hosts or groups. It is simple, readable and ideal for stable environments. A dynamic inventory is produced at run time by an inventory plugin or script that queries a source of truth, such as AWS EC2, Azure, GCP, VMware, OpenStack or a CMDB, so the host list follows reality as instances come and go. Plugins usually build groups from tags, regions or other metadata with keyed groups and compose variables. In practice I combine them: dynamic sources for cloud fleets, static files for fixed infrastructure, and a directory containing both. I keep group_vars and host_vars beside the inventory, and use ansible-inventory with the graph or list options to verify what Ansible sees before running anything.
f: How do keyed groups work in a cloud inventory plugin?
How do you verify what an inventory resolves to?
p: Static inventories are files listing hosts and groups; dynamic inventories use plugins to query AWS, Azure, VMware or a CMDB at run time. Combine both in a directory and check results with ansible-inventory.
tip: Say you verify with ansible-inventory before any run.

q: When do you use ad-hoc commands rather than playbooks?
a: Ad-hoc commands run a single module against a set of hosts from the command line, with no file to write. They are ideal for quick, one-off operational tasks: checking connectivity with the ping module, gathering facts, checking disk space, restarting a service on a few hosts during an incident, copying a file, or testing that a new module and credentials work. Anything that should be repeated, reviewed, versioned or run by someone else belongs in a playbook, because playbooks document intent, can be code reviewed, are repeatable across environments and support handlers, loops, conditionals and variables. My rule is that an ad-hoc command is fine for investigation and for emergencies, but if I run the same command twice I turn it into a playbook or role. I also take care with the command and shell modules ad hoc, since they are not idempotent and I prefer purpose-built modules.
f: Why avoid shell in ad-hoc commands?
How would you restart a service on 5 hosts quickly and safely?
p: Ad-hoc commands suit quick investigation or incident actions with one module. Repeatable or shared work goes into a playbook, which is reviewable, versioned and supports variables, handlers and conditionals.
tip: Say if you run it twice, it becomes a playbook.

q: What does idempotency mean in Ansible and how do you keep tasks idempotent?
a: Idempotency means running a task repeatedly leads to the same end state, and a second run reports no changes. Most core modules achieve this by describing desired state, for example the package module with state present, the file module with a mode, or the service module with state started. Each checks current state first and acts only if different. It matters because it makes playbooks safe to rerun, supports drift correction, and lets you trust the changed count as a signal. Problems arise with the command, shell and raw modules, which always report changed unless told otherwise. I fix that with creates or removes arguments, changed_when and failed_when conditions, or by replacing them with proper modules. I also verify by running twice in CI and expecting zero changes on the second run, and use check mode with diff to preview. Non-idempotent tasks hide real drift and cause noisy handlers.
f: How do you make a shell task report changed correctly?
How would you test idempotency in CI?
p: Idempotent tasks converge to the same state on every run, so a second run reports zero changes. Prefer state-based modules, use creates, changed_when and failed_when for command tasks, and test by running twice.
tip: Mention the run-twice test in CI.

q: How does Ansible compare with Puppet, Chef and Terraform, and where does each fit?
a: Ansible is agentless and push-based, uses YAML and is easy to start with, so it is strong for orchestration, ad-hoc operations and configuration of existing machines. Puppet and Chef use agents that pull configuration from a server on a schedule, with a declarative language in Puppet and Ruby-based recipes in Chef, which gives continuous enforcement and drift correction at large scale but needs infrastructure to run. Terraform is different in kind: it provisions and manages the lifecycle of infrastructure resources such as networks, instances and managed services, tracking them in state, while Ansible is better at what happens inside the machine afterwards. A common pattern is Terraform to create infrastructure and Ansible to configure it, or to bake images with Packer and Ansible. There is overlap, since Ansible has cloud modules and Terraform has provisioners, so I choose by the lifecycle: create and destroy with Terraform, configure and operate with Ansible.
f: Why not use Ansible for all provisioning?
What is the drawback of a pull-based agent model?
p: Ansible is agentless, push-based and strong for orchestration and configuration. Puppet and Chef are agent-based pull tools with continuous enforcement. Terraform manages infrastructure lifecycle with state; use it to create, and Ansible to configure.
tip: Say Terraform creates, Ansible configures.

q: How does Ansible choose configuration, and what is the precedence of ansible.cfg?
a: Ansible reads settings from several places, and the first match wins rather than merging. The order is the ANSIBLE_CONFIG environment variable, then ansible.cfg in the current directory, then a hidden ansible.cfg in the user's home, then the system file in etc. Individual settings can also be overridden by environment variables such as ANSIBLE_FORKS and by command line flags, which take priority. Because the current directory file is picked up, a project-level ansible.cfg checked into the repository makes behaviour reproducible for the team and in CI, including the inventory path, roles path, remote user, forks, pipelining, callbacks and the collections path. One security detail: Ansible ignores a configuration file in a world-writable directory, to prevent hijacking. I use ansible-config dump with the only-changed option to see which values are in effect and where they came from, which is the fastest way to debug surprising behaviour.
f: Why is a world-writable ansible.cfg ignored?
How do you see the effective configuration?
p: The first config found wins: ANSIBLE_CONFIG, then ansible.cfg in the current directory, home, then system. Environment variables and flags override. Keep a project ansible.cfg in the repo and inspect with ansible-config dump.
tip: Mention a repo-level ansible.cfg for reproducibility.

q: What are facts, and when would you disable or customise fact gathering?
a: Facts are system information that Ansible collects from each host at the start of a play using the setup module, such as operating system, distribution, network interfaces, memory and mounts. They are available as variables, for example ansible_facts distribution or ansible_default_ipv4, and let playbooks adapt to different platforms. Gathering costs a round trip and a second or more per host, which is significant at scale. I disable it with gather_facts false when a play needs none, or limit it with gather_subset to only what I use, such as min or network. Fact caching with a backend like Redis or JSON files avoids recomputing across runs. I can also write custom facts as files on the host in the facts.d directory, which Ansible exposes under ansible_local, useful for exposing application or compliance data. I prefer the ansible_facts dictionary over injected top-level variables for clarity.
f: How does fact caching speed up large runs?
What are local facts?
p: Facts are host details gathered by the setup module at play start and used as variables. Disable them or limit with gather_subset to save time, cache them for large fleets, and add custom facts under facts.d.
tip: Say gather_subset and caching are the scale levers.

q: How do connection methods and privilege escalation (become) work?
a: Ansible connects through a connection plugin: SSH by default for Linux and network devices using paramiko or OpenSSH, WinRM or SSH for Windows, local for the control node, and docker or kubectl style plugins for containers. Authentication is normally by SSH keys through an agent, with the remote user set in inventory, config or play. Privilege escalation is controlled by become: when true, tasks run through sudo by default, or su, doas and others, as the become user, root unless specified, and the become password can be supplied or sudo can be passwordless for the automation account. I set become at play level only where needed rather than globally, and use become_user for application accounts. Good practice is a dedicated automation user, key-based authentication, restricted sudoers entries where feasible, and a bastion through ProxyCommand or ansible_ssh_common_args when hosts are in private networks.
f: How would you reach hosts behind a bastion?
What is the risk of passwordless sudo for all commands?
p: Connection plugins such as SSH or WinRM reach hosts; become escalates with sudo or su. Use a dedicated automation user with keys, apply become only where needed, and use a bastion through ProxyCommand for private networks.
cmds:
- hosts: db
  become: true
  become_user: postgres
tip: Say least privilege: become only on tasks that need it.

q: What is the difference between modules, plugins and collections?
a: A module is a unit of work that runs on the target host, such as copy, apt, user or service, and returns structured results. A plugin extends Ansible itself and runs on the control node: connection plugins, lookup plugins, filter plugins, callback plugins, inventory plugins and strategy plugins, among others. So modules do the managed work, while plugins change how Ansible connects, reads data, formats output or processes variables. A collection is a distribution format that bundles modules, plugins, roles, playbooks and documentation under a namespace, for example amazon.aws or kubernetes.core, versioned and installed from Galaxy, Automation Hub or a private source. Since ansible-core 2.10 most content lives in collections, so the core package stays small and content releases independently. In playbooks I use fully qualified collection names like ansible.builtin.copy to avoid ambiguity, and pin collection versions in requirements.yml for reproducible runs.
f: Where do lookup plugins run?
Why pin collection versions?
p: Modules run on targets and do the work. Plugins run on the control node and extend connections, lookups, filters and callbacks. Collections package modules, plugins and roles under a namespace and are versioned and pinned in requirements.yml.
tip: Say modules run on targets, plugins on the controller.

q: What is the difference between ansible-core and the Ansible community package, and how do you manage versions?
a: Ansible-core is the engine: the command line tools, the language, the built-in collection and the plugin framework. The community Ansible package, sometimes called the batteries-included distribution, bundles ansible-core with a curated set of collections, so a single install gives you many modules. Red Hat's Ansible Automation Platform is a supported product with certified collections, execution environments and a controller. Version management matters because modules and syntax change: each ansible-core release supports a range of Python versions on the control node and on targets, and old targets may need an older interpreter. I pin ansible-core and collection versions in a requirements file, ideally packaged in an execution environment container image, so laptops, CI and the controller all run the same versions. Upgrades are tested in a branch with ansible-lint and Molecule, and I read the porting guides before moving to a new major release.
f: What breaks when upgrading ansible-core?
Why use an execution environment image?
p: Ansible-core is the engine and built-ins; the community package adds many collections. Pin ansible-core and collection versions, ideally in an execution environment image, and test upgrades with lint and Molecule before rollout.
tip: Say pin versions and package them in an execution environment.

q: Describe the structure of a playbook, plays and tasks.
a: A playbook is a YAML file containing a list of plays. Each play maps a group of hosts to a set of tasks and defines settings such as the remote user, become, variables, gather_facts and tags. Within a play, execution is ordered: pre_tasks, then roles, then tasks, then post_tasks, with handlers notified along the way and run at defined points. Each task calls one module with arguments, may have a name, conditions, loops, register, tags, delegation, error handling and notify. Tasks run in order against all hosts in the play in parallel, up to the forks limit, using the linear strategy by default, so every host completes a task before the next starts. Good style is to give every task a descriptive name, keep plays short by moving logic into roles, use fully qualified module names, keep YAML valid and indent consistently, and put variables in group_vars rather than inside the play.
f: In what order do pre_tasks, roles and tasks run?
What does the linear strategy mean?
p: A playbook is a list of plays; each play targets hosts, sets options and runs pre_tasks, roles, tasks and post_tasks in order. Tasks call modules, run across hosts in parallel, and notify handlers. Keep plays short and named.
cmds:
- name: Configure web
  hosts: web
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      ansible.builtin.package:
        name: nginx
        state: present
tip: Say name every task and push logic into roles.

q: How do handlers work and what are the pitfalls?
a: Handlers are tasks that run only when notified by another task that reported a change, typically to restart or reload a service after its configuration file changed. Multiple notifications of the same handler result in a single run, and handlers run at the end of the play by default, in the order they are defined, not the order they were notified. This design avoids restarting a service several times. Pitfalls include a handler not running because the notifying task failed before the end of the play, since by default a failure stops the flow and skips handlers unless force_handlers is set. Another is needing the restart earlier, in the middle of a play, which you handle with the meta flush_handlers task. Handlers also only fire on change, so a first run that fails halfway can leave a changed file with no restart on the next run, and listen topics allow one notification to trigger several handlers.
f: Why might a handler not run after a failure?
How do you force a handler to run mid-play?
p: Handlers run once at the end of a play when notified by changed tasks, in definition order. Use meta flush_handlers to run earlier, force_handlers to run after failures, and listen to group handlers.
cmds:
- name: Update config
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: app.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/app.conf
  notify: Restart app
tip: Mention flush_handlers and the failed-play pitfall.

q: How do loops work in Ansible, and when should you avoid them?
a: The loop keyword repeats a task over a list, exposing each element as the item variable, which can be renamed with loop_control and loop_var. Loops can iterate over simple lists, lists of dictionaries, dictionaries converted with the dict2items filter, or results from lookups and filters such as subelements and product. You can add labels to keep output readable, a pause for rate limits, and an index variable. Older with_ keywords still work but loop is preferred. I avoid loops when the module already accepts a list, for example the package module accepts many names in one call, which is much faster since it runs once rather than once per item. Another problem is loops with register, which return a results list, and large loops over big data in Jinja, which are slow. Also nested loops in included tasks need loop_var set to avoid clashes with the outer item.
f: Why does loop_var matter in nested includes?
How do you loop over a dictionary?
p: Use loop with item, loop_control for labels and renamed variables, dict2items for dictionaries. Avoid loops where a module accepts a list, such as package, since one call is faster than many.
cmds:
- name: Create users
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: "{{ item.name }}"
    groups: "{{ item.groups }}"
  loop: "{{ users }}"
  loop_control:
    label: "{{ item.name }}"
tip: Say pass a list to the module instead of looping where possible.

q: How do conditionals with when and failed_when and changed_when work?
a: The when keyword runs a task only if a Jinja2 expression is true, written without double curly braces, for example when ansible_os_family equals Debian, or when a registered variable is defined or contains a string. Conditions can combine with and, or and not, and a list of conditions means all must be true. On loops, when is evaluated per item. The failed_when keyword overrides what counts as a failure, useful when a command returns a nonzero code that is acceptable or prints an error message with a zero exit code. Similarly changed_when controls whether the task reports a change, which is essential for making command and shell tasks idempotent and for accurate handler notification. Common mistakes include comparing strings and booleans loosely, forgetting that variables from the command line are strings, and using when with an undefined variable without the default filter. I also use the is defined, is changed and is failed tests for clarity.
f: How do you treat a registered result as failed on certain output?
Why do command-line booleans cause problems?
p: when runs a task on a true expression; failed_when and changed_when redefine failure and change for tasks such as command. Use defaults for undefined variables and watch for string versus boolean types.
cmds:
- ansible.builtin.command: /usr/local/bin/check_app
  register: r
  failed_when: "'CRITICAL' in r.stdout"
  changed_when: false
tip: Say changed_when false for read-only commands.

q: How do you handle errors with block, rescue and always, and ignore_errors?
a: A block groups tasks so they share conditions, privilege settings and error handling. The rescue section runs if any task in the block fails, similar to catch, and the always section runs regardless, similar to finally. The pattern lets you attempt a risky operation, such as a deployment, roll back in rescue, and always send a notification or clean up in always. After a successful rescue the play continues for that host and the host is not marked failed, though the failure is shown in the output. The ignore_errors keyword simply continues past a failing task but hides real problems, so I use it sparingly and prefer targeted failed_when conditions. Related controls are any_errors_fatal to stop all hosts on a failure, max_fail_percentage for rolling deployments, and ignore_unreachable. Inside rescue, the ansible_failed_task and ansible_failed_result variables describe what failed, which helps with diagnostics.
f: What variables are available inside rescue?
When would you use any_errors_fatal?
p: block groups tasks; rescue handles failures and always runs regardless, like try, catch and finally. Prefer this and targeted failed_when over ignore_errors, and use any_errors_fatal or max_fail_percentage for rolling changes.
tip: Say rescue for rollback, always for cleanup.

q: How are tags used, and what are the best practices?
a: Tags label tasks, blocks, roles and plays so you can run or skip a subset of a playbook with the tags and skip-tags options, for example only configuration changes or only the deployment step. Special tags include always, which runs unless skipped explicitly, and never, plus tagged, untagged and all. Tags applied to a role or an include are inherited by the contained tasks differently depending on whether it is a static import or dynamic include, which is a frequent source of confusion: with include_role you need the apply keyword to pass tags to the inner tasks. Best practice is a small, documented vocabulary such as packages, config, deploy and security, rather than ad-hoc tags, and using list-tags to document them. I do not rely on tags for safety, because a partial run may leave things inconsistent, and full runs in CI remain the source of truth. Tags are great for fast iteration during development.
f: How do tags behave with include_role?
What does the always tag do?
p: Tags let you run or skip subsets with --tags and --skip-tags. Imports inherit tags, dynamic includes need apply. Keep a small documented tag vocabulary and rely on full runs in CI.
tip: Mention the import versus include difference.

q: What do delegate_to, run_once and local_action do, and when do you use them?
a: The delegate_to keyword runs a task on a different host than the one being iterated, while still using the original host's variables. It is used for actions that must happen elsewhere: removing a host from a load balancer from the control node before updating it, updating a DNS record through an API, or registering with a monitoring server. With delegate_to localhost, tasks run on the control node, and local_action is a shorthand for that. The run_once keyword executes a task a single time for the whole play, on the first host in the batch, for example one database migration or sending one notification, and the result is shared with all hosts. Cautions are that run_once with serial applies per batch, that delegated tasks use facts of the original host unless delegate_facts is set, and that connection and become settings apply to the delegate target, so credentials must work there.
f: How does run_once behave with serial?
What is delegate_facts?
p: delegate_to runs a task on another host while keeping the current host's variables, for load balancer, DNS or monitoring calls. run_once executes a task once per play or batch. Watch serial interactions and delegated credentials.
cmds:
- name: Drain from LB
  ansible.builtin.uri:
    url: "https://lb/api/drain/{{ inventory_hostname }}"
    method: POST
  delegate_to: localhost
tip: Say run_once applies per serial batch.

q: How do check mode and diff mode work, and what are their limits?
a: Check mode, enabled with the check option, simulates a run: modules that support it report what would change without changing anything. Diff mode, enabled with the diff option, shows a before and after comparison for files and templates. Together they give a dry run for review, useful in change approval and in pull request pipelines. The limits are important: modules that do not support check mode are skipped or report nothing, command and shell tasks are skipped by default unless a check_mode override is set, and later tasks that depend on earlier changes or registered output may fail or show misleading results because the earlier change never happened. You can mark a task with check_mode true or false to force behaviour, for example to run a read-only command even in check mode. So check mode is a strong signal rather than a guarantee, and I still verify in a staging environment before production.
f: Why do some tasks fail only in check mode?
How do you force a command to run in check mode?
p: Check mode simulates changes and diff mode shows file differences, giving a reviewable dry run. Limits include modules without support, skipped command tasks and dependent tasks, so treat it as a signal, not a guarantee.
cmds:
- ansible.builtin.command: cat /etc/app.conf
  check_mode: false
  changed_when: false
tip: Say dry-run is advisory; staging remains the proof.

q: What is the difference between command, shell, raw and script modules?
a: The command module runs a command without a shell, so pipes, redirects, environment expansion and operators do not work, which also makes it safer against injection. The shell module runs through a shell, supporting pipes and redirects, with more risk if variables contain untrusted input. The raw module sends the command straight over SSH without needing Python on the target, useful for bootstrapping a host that lacks Python or for network devices. The script module copies a local script to the target and runs it there. None of them is idempotent by default, so each always reports changed unless you use creates or removes, changed_when or failed_when. My order of preference is: a dedicated module first, then command, then shell only when a shell feature is truly required, and then I quote variables carefully with the quote filter. Raw is used only for bootstrap, such as installing Python.
f: When is raw appropriate?
How do you protect shell tasks from injection?
p: command runs without a shell and is safer; shell allows pipes but risks injection; raw needs no Python and suits bootstrapping; script copies and runs a local script. Prefer proper modules and make these idempotent with creates, removes and changed_when.
tip: Say a module first, then command, shell last.

q: What is the difference between include and import for tasks and roles?
a: Imports are static: the import_tasks and import_role statements are processed when the playbook is parsed, so the content is pre-loaded, tags and conditionals are applied to every contained task, and you can list all tasks with list-tasks. Includes are dynamic: include_tasks and include_role are processed when execution reaches them, so file names and loops can use runtime variables, and the included content is not visible to list-tasks. When a condition is attached, with an import it is copied to each inner task, with an include it is evaluated once and gates the whole include. Tags behave differently too: tags on an include apply to the include itself unless you use apply. I use imports for fixed structure because they are predictable, and includes when the file or role depends on facts, loops or conditions known only at run time. Mixing them without understanding this causes skipped tasks and tag surprises.
f: Which one supports looping?
Why might tags seem to be ignored on an include?
p: Import is static, processed at parse time, applying tags and conditions to inner tasks. Include is dynamic, evaluated at run time, so it supports loops and variable file names. Use imports for fixed structure and includes for runtime decisions.
tip: Say static for structure, dynamic for runtime choices.

q: What is the structure of an Ansible role and why use roles?
a: A role is a standard directory layout for reusable automation. Key directories are tasks with main.yml as the entry point, handlers, defaults for low-precedence variables meant to be overridden, vars for high-precedence internal values, templates for Jinja2 files, files for static files, meta for dependencies and metadata, and optionally library, module_utils and tests. Roles let you package one capability, such as an nginx setup or a hardening baseline, and reuse it across playbooks, teams and environments with different variables. They improve readability because playbooks become short lists of roles, enable testing in isolation with Molecule, and can be shared through collections or Galaxy. Good practice is one role per clear responsibility, a documented README with variables, defaults for everything configurable, prefixing variable names with the role name to avoid collisions, no hidden dependencies, and idempotent, platform-aware tasks.
f: Why prefix variables with the role name?
What belongs in defaults versus vars?
p: A role has tasks, handlers, defaults, vars, templates, files and meta. It packages one capability for reuse and isolated testing. Keep one responsibility, document variables, prefix names and put overridable values in defaults.
tip: Say prefix variables to avoid collisions.

q: How do role dependencies work and what are their pitfalls?
a: Dependencies are declared in the role's meta main file as a list of other roles that must run first, optionally with parameters. When the playbook applies the role, Ansible executes the dependencies before it, and by default each dependency runs only once even if several roles list it, unless allow_duplicates is set. They are useful for shared prerequisites such as a common baseline or a repository setup role. Pitfalls include hidden coupling that makes a role harder to understand and test alone, ordering surprises when dependencies pull in tasks the playbook author did not expect, variable precedence changes because dependency parameters are applied as role variables, and difficulty when a dependency comes from another collection. Many teams prefer explicit composition: the playbook lists roles in order, or a higher-level role uses include_role, so the flow is visible. I keep dependencies minimal, documented and version-pinned in requirements.yml.
f: What does allow_duplicates do?
Why prefer explicit role ordering in the playbook?
p: Dependencies in meta main run before a role and execute once by default unless allow_duplicates is set. They hide coupling and affect variable precedence, so keep them minimal and often compose roles explicitly in the playbook.
cmds:
# roles/app/meta/main.yml
dependencies:
  - role: common
  - role: nginx
    vars:
      nginx_port: 8080
tip: Say explicit composition is clearer than hidden dependencies.

q: What are Ansible collections and how do you use and publish them?
a: A collection is a versioned package that can contain modules, plugins, roles, playbooks and docs under a namespace dot name identifier. Users install them with ansible-galaxy collection install, from Galaxy, Red Hat Automation Hub, a private Automation Hub or a Git repository, and list them in requirements.yml with version constraints. In playbooks you call content by its fully qualified collection name, or declare a collections search path. To publish, you create the skeleton with ansible-galaxy collection init, write a galaxy.yml with the namespace, name, version and dependencies, build with ansible-galaxy collection build, and publish the tarball with an API token. Teams often host internal collections in a private registry to share company roles, modules and filter plugins. I use semantic versioning, changelogs, sanity tests with ansible-test, and CI to build and release, and I pin consumers to a version range to avoid surprise breakages.
f: What goes in galaxy.yml?
How do you host a private collection?
p: A collection bundles modules, plugins and roles under a namespace and version. Install from Galaxy or a private hub via requirements.yml, call by fully qualified name, and publish with galaxy.yml, ansible-galaxy build and publish, with ansible-test in CI.
cmds: ansible-galaxy collection build && ansible-galaxy collection publish myorg-platform-1.2.0.tar.gz
tip: Say semantic versions and a pinned requirements file.

q: How do you use Galaxy and requirements.yml to manage dependencies reproducibly?
a: The requirements.yml file lists the roles and collections a project needs, with sources and versions, so anyone can install exactly the same content. For collections you give a name and a version constraint, and optionally a source or server, and for roles you can reference Galaxy names or Git URLs with a tag or commit. Installing is one command, and I set the collections and roles paths in ansible.cfg to a project-local directory, so nothing depends on what happens to be installed globally. For reproducibility I pin exact versions or narrow ranges, avoid tracking a moving branch in production, and use a private Automation Hub or mirror so builds do not depend on public availability. In CI, I install from the file in a clean environment before linting and testing. For enterprise setups, the same requirements file feeds ansible-builder to create an execution environment image, so the controller uses identical content.
f: Why avoid pinning to a branch?
How does requirements.yml feed an execution environment?
p: requirements.yml pins the roles and collections a project needs. Install into a project-local path, pin versions or commits, use a private mirror, and reuse the file to build execution environment images so every environment matches.
tip: Say pin versions and mirror privately for reproducibility.

q: When should logic be a role, a collection or a custom module?
a: I choose by what the reuse looks like. A role is the right unit to reuse a sequence of tasks that configures something, such as installing and configuring a service. A collection is the packaging and distribution layer: when I have several related roles, plugins or modules, or content shared across teams, I put them in a collection with versioning. A custom module is appropriate when the work needs real programming logic or an API that existing modules do not cover, or when a complex task in YAML becomes unreadable and not idempotent. Modules written in Python give structured arguments, check mode support, proper change detection and documentation, while a long chain of shell commands does not. Before writing anything new, I search existing collections, because maintained modules beat custom code. If I do write one, I test with ansible-test and unit tests and keep it small and well documented.
f: What makes a custom module better than a shell chain?
What does a module need to support check mode?
p: Use a role for reusable task sequences, a collection to package and version related content, and a custom module when you need real logic, an uncovered API, or proper idempotency and check mode. Search existing collections first.
tip: Say look for an existing module before writing one.

q: Why use fully qualified collection names, and how do you migrate old playbooks?
a: Fully qualified collection names, such as ansible.builtin.copy or amazon.aws.ec2_instance, remove ambiguity about which module runs. Without them, Ansible searches namespaces, and a collection added later could shadow a module of the same short name, changing behaviour silently. They also make it obvious where documentation and fixes live and which collection must be installed. Migration is mostly mechanical: ansible-lint has a fqcn rule that detects short names and can auto-fix many of them, and tools like the ansible-core migration notes list the mapping of old module names to collections. I update playbooks and roles, add the needed collections to requirements.yml with versions, run lint and Molecule, and test on a staging inventory. The effort is worth it because pinned, qualified content makes runs reproducible and upgrades of ansible-core much less risky.
f: What can happen without FQCN when a new collection is installed?
How does ansible-lint help migrate?
p: FQCNs such as ansible.builtin.copy remove ambiguity and shadowing risk and show which collection is required. Migrate with ansible-lint fqcn rule, add collections to requirements.yml and test in staging.
tip: Say lint can auto-fix most short names.

q: How do you write a custom Ansible module, and what makes it good?
a: A custom module is usually a Python file placed in a library directory next to a playbook or role, or inside a collection. It uses the AnsibleModule helper to declare an argument specification with types, required flags, choices and defaults, reads the parameters, does the work, and exits with exit_json including changed and any result data, or fail_json with a message. A good module is idempotent: it checks the current state, compares to the desired state and changes only if needed. It supports check mode by declaring that and not applying changes, it never prints secrets, marks sensitive parameters with no_log, handles errors with clear messages, and includes documentation in the DOCUMENTATION, EXAMPLES and RETURN strings so ansible-doc works. I test with ansible-test sanity and units, and mock external calls. Module code runs on the target, so dependencies must be available there, otherwise consider an action plugin or a lookup running locally.
f: How do you support check mode?
How do you hide secret parameters?
p: Write a Python file using AnsibleModule with an argument spec, compute current versus desired state, return exit_json with changed, support check mode, use no_log for secrets, and document with DOCUMENTATION, EXAMPLES and RETURN. Test with ansible-test.
tip: Say idempotent, check-mode aware and documented.
